title: Soloing over Chords
intro: Improvising on the guitar is choosing notes that fit the chord of the moment. Scale boxes give you a safe set of notes; chord tones, arpeggios and expressive bends make the line sound as if it knows where the harmony is going.

blocks.text: The minor pentatonic box (see Scales on the Guitar (#/arts/guitar/guitar-theory/scales)) works over a whole minor-key song or a blues, because it contains no strong clashes with the tonic chord. Over a 12-bar blues in A, A minor pentatonic over A7, D7 and E7 is the classic sound of blues-rock: its C clashes with A7's C♯ on purpose (the 'blue' third), and players bend it up towards C♯.

A line that lands on a chord tone (root, 3rd, 5th or 7th) on a strong beat sounds 'inside' the harmony; a line that keeps landing on other notes sounds vague. The most telling targets are the 3rd and 7th, which change from chord to chord (see guide tones (#/arts/music-theory/jazz-harmony)). Over A7 to D7 in the blues, C♯ (3rd of A7) to C (7th of D7) is a half-step that spells the chord change in one move.

widget.title: Over A7 → D7: the 3rd of A7 falls to the 7th of D7

examples.label: Chords with the guide-tone line on top

blocks.text: An arpeggio plays a chord's notes one at a time. Each CAGED shape contains an arpeggio in its position; practising arpeggios of the progression's chords in one position teaches the hands where the chord tones are while the scale stays the same. Jazz guitarists build solos from arpeggios of the chords and of their upper structures (the 3rd-to-9th of a seventh chord makes a new seventh chord: Cmaj7's E G B D is Em7).

blocks.text: Bends, slides and vibrato as pitch

On the piano a note has one pitch. On the guitar a bend moves continuously between pitches, so the guitarist can play the in-between notes of the blues and aim a note at a chord tone: bending the 2nd up a whole step to the 3rd, or the 4th to the 5th. A bend that is out of tune is the guitar's most obvious wrong note; practise bending to a target you have just played on the next fret.

blocks.title: Targets
blocks.text: In a ii–V–I in C (Dm7–G7–Cmaj7), which notes make a smooth guide-tone line starting on F?
solution: F is the 3rd of Dm7. It stays as the 7th of G7 (F), then falls a half step to E, the 3rd of Cmaj7: F–F–E.

blocks.title: Blues bend
blocks.text: Over an E7 chord in the E blues, which note in E minor pentatonic is usually bent towards the major third, and to what?
solution: E minor pentatonic is E G A B D. The minor third G is bent up a half step towards G♯, the major third of E7 (often only a quarter-tone, the 'blue' third).

blocks.text: Sources: Goodrick, M. (1987). The Advancing Guitarist. Hal Leonard; Levine, M. (1995). The Jazz Theory Book. Sher Music; Kolb, T. (2005). Blues Guitar Method. Hal Leonard.
